1.title: Fact-Checking, Validation and Human Review
1.text: Welcome to Module four: Fact-Checking, Validation and Human Review. This module covers fact-checking, validation and human review. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. The main fact-checking techniques: primary sources, grounding, cross-checking, recalculation, sampling. How to use web search and citations safely. How much checking an output needs, based on stakes. When a human must review before anything is sent, published or decided.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedarbrook's Press Release
1.text: Our running case is Cedarbrook Outfitters. Cedarbrook's Press Release. Communications asks Claude to draft a release on the company's carbon-reduction results. The draft contains three statistics and a quote attributed to an industry body. Before publishing, the team traces each number to the sustainability report and each quote to the original.

1.title: Fact-Checking Techniques
1.text: Fact-Checking Techniques. Check the primary source. How it works: Open the official document, regulation, dataset or website and compare. Best for: Citations, legal and policy statements, quotes. Ground Claude in your documents. How it works: Upload or paste the source and tell Claude to answer only from it and to quote the supporting lines. Best for: Summaries and Q and A on known material. Ask for sources, then check them. How it works: Request links or titles; open them yourself; a source Claude cannot supply is a red flag. Best for: Research claims. Cross-check with independent sources. How it works: Confirm key facts in two or more trustworthy places. Best for: Statistics, market facts, dates.

1.title: Fact-Checking Techniques, continued
1.text: Fact-Checking Techniques, continued. Recalculate. How it works: Redo totals and percentages from the raw data in a spreadsheet. Best for: Numbers and tables. Spot-check a sample. How it works: Check a random subset of items against the source; widen if errors appear. Best for: Long lists, bulk summaries. Test the artifact. How it works: Run the formula, script or macro on sample data with a known answer. Best for: Technical outputs. Second pair of eyes. How it works: A colleague or subject-matter expert reviews. Best for: High-stakes content.

1.title: Fact-Checking Techniques, continued
1.text: Fact-Checking Techniques, continued. The figure shows this: A ladder of verification strength: sounds right is weakest; checking a primary source and expert review are strongest. Asking Claude "are you sure?" is not verification: it may repeat the error or change a correct answer. Asking Claude to find problems in its own draft is a useful first pass, but not a substitute for your check against a source.

1.title: Fact-Checking Techniques, continued
1.text: Fact-Checking Techniques, continued. Quote-first prompting: "First extract the exact lines that answer the question, then answer." This makes unsupported claims easier to spot. Allow "I don't know": tell Claude it may answer "the document does not say" instead of guessing. Exam tip: The strongest checks go outside Claude: an authoritative source, a recalculation, a test run or a qualified person.

1.title: Using Web Search and Citations
1.text: Using Web Search and Citations. With web search on, Claude grounds answers in live web content and gives citations and source links. A visible indicator shows when it is searching. Review the cited sources. The Help Center warns that original sites may hold context or detail not in Claude's synthesis, and that answer quality depends on the sources it used. Ask for multiple sources and verify important information against authoritative ones. Prefer primary and official sources (regulators, standards bodies, the company itself) over blogs. Dates matter: check how recent a source is.

1.title: Using Web Search and Citations, continued
1.text: Using Web Search and Citations, continued. Include "search the web" in the prompt to make sure it searches, or tell it not to when you want it to use only your documents. Research mode produces a longer report with citations; the same rule applies: open the sources for the claims you will rely on.

1.title: Using Web Search and Citations, continued
1.text: Using Web Search and Citations, continued. The figure shows this: Citations make checking possible: follow them to the source and confirm the claim. Exam tip: A cited answer is easier to verify, not already verified. The step that counts is that a person reads the source.

1.title: How Much Checking Is Enough?
1.text: How Much Checking Is Enough? Match the depth of review to the risk. Stakes. Lower risk: Internal brainstorm. Higher risk: Legal, medical, financial, safety, people decisions. Audience. Lower risk: You alone. Higher risk: Customers, regulators, the public, the board. Reversibility. Lower risk: Easy to fix. Higher risk: Sent, published, filed, paid. Source reliability. Lower risk: You provided and trust the source. Higher risk: Claude answered from memory. Novelty. Lower risk: Routine, repeated task with a proven prompt. Higher risk: New topic or unfamiliar domain.

1.title: How Much Checking Is Enough?, continued
1.text: How Much Checking Is Enough?, continued. The figure shows this: Review depth grows with stakes and with how hard the output is to undo. Low stakes and reversible (a brainstorm list): a quick read. Medium (an internal report): spot-check the key figures. High and hard to undo (a regulatory filing, a customer-facing claim, a contract summary): check every claim and add expert review.

1.title: When Human Review Is Required
1.text: When Human Review Is Required. A qualified human must review before use when. The output supports legal, medical, financial, safety or compliance decisions. It affects people: hiring, promotion, credit, benefits, grades, access to services. It will be published or sent externally under the company's name. It involves regulated or sensitive data (Module thirteen). The action is irreversible or costly (payments, deletions, sending to many customers). Claude's answer is uncertain, contradictory or outside the checker's expertise. Organizational policy says so.

1.title: When Human Review Is Required, continued
1.text: When Human Review Is Required, continued. Anthropic's Usage Policy lists high-risk uses (legal, medical, finance, credit, insurance, housing, employment, education, public benefits). For these a qualified human-in-the-loop must meaningfully review the recommendation before it is delivered or acted on and must be able to change it, and the affected person must be told A I was involved. The human must be qualified: a lawyer reviews legal text, an accountant reviews financial figures. Skimming is not review. Document how A I was used and who reviewed the result. Keep the person accountable: Claude drafts; the human owns the decision. Exam tip: In scenarios about regulated advice, people decisions or external publication, the right answer includes review by a qualified person before use, never "send it, Claude is usually right".

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Strongest checks: Primary source, recalculation, test run, qualified reviewer. Weak checks: "Are you sure?", polish, self-rated confidence. Grounding: Answer only from the provided source; quote lines; allow "not covered". Web search: Citations help; open the sources; prefer primary and recent. Depth: Scale with stakes, audience, reversibility, source reliability, novelty. Human review needed: Legal, medical, financial, safety, people decisions, external publication, regulated data, irreversible actions, policy. High-risk uses: Qualified human reviews and can change it; tell affected people A I was involved. Accountability: Claude drafts; a named person decides.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A press release draft contains a statistic and a quote attributed to a trade body. What is the best validation? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Verify claims against the original sources, especially for external publication.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which prompt best reduces unsupported claims when summarizing an uploaded policy? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Grounding in the document, quoting and allowing "not covered" make errors visible.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An associate asks Claude "are you sure?" and Claude says yes. What does that prove? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Self-reported certainty is not a validation method, so the claim still has to be checked against an independent source.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Claude's web-search answer includes citations. What is the best next step for a claim you will rely on? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Citations make verification possible; a person must follow them.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which output needs the deepest review? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. External, contract-related content carries high stakes and is hard to undo.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Select two. Which two situations require review by a qualified human before use? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Medical guidance and employment decisions are high-risk uses that need a qualified human reviewer.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Claude produces a spreadsheet formula for commission calculations. What is the best validation? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Test technical outputs on known cases before real use.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Why should a human reviewer of a legal summary be qualified? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Review is only meaningful when the reviewer can recognize substantive errors.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. A team uses Claude to draft decision letters about benefits. What does the Usage Policy expect? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. High-risk uses need human-in-the-loop review and disclosure that A I was involved.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all nine answers. Question one: C. Question two: B. Question three: A. Question four: B. Question five: D. Question six: B and D. Question seven: D. Question eight: D. Question nine: A. In the next module, we continue the course.
